An 81-year-old man initially developed a cough, subjective fever, and shortness of breath. He was first treated with azithromycin for bronchitis, followed by levofloxacin after a right upper lobe infiltrate was found. His symptoms progressed despite antibiotics. Medical history includes coronary artery disease with coronary artery bypass (two years prior), atrial fibrillation on rivaroxaban, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c: 8.1%). He had spent time at a Northern Minnesota cabin but reported minimal outdoor exposure. Previous missionary work in Colombia ended two years before admission. Never smoked and rarely consumed alcohol.

Cardiac examination showed tachycardic irregularly irregular rhythm, systolic ejection murmur, and mild pitting edema to the knee bilaterally. No cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. clinical_record:
A 9-month-old spayed female Ragdoll cat was evaluated for 5 days of persistent vomiting and one episode of hematemesis, along with reduced appetite and lethargy. The cat’s history was unremarkable; it had been fed a raw rabbit–based raw food (BARF) diet for 3 months. On examination, the cat was moderately dehydrated (≈7%), febrile (39.9°C), with pale mucous membranes (capillary refill time ~3 s) and mild discomfort on abdominal palpation; body condition score was 4/9 (4.2 kg). Complete blood count, serum biochemistry, and FIV/FeLV tests were within normal limits or negative. Thoracic and abdominal radiographs were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed multiple rounded, echogenic neoformations at the pyloric antrum and mild mesenteric lymphadenomegaly; the remainder of the abdomen appeared normal. Intravenous fluids and omeprazole were initiated. Endoscopy showed several sessile, smooth-surfaced nodules (0.5–2 cm) in the pyloric antrum; the duodenum was normal. Cytological brushing of the gastric mucosa demonstrated mucosal cells, mixed neutrophilic and macrophagic inflammation, and occasional large, non-septate hyphae with irregular diameter and branching. Pending histology, the cat was treated with fluids, omeprazole, maropitant, sucralfate, and ketoconazole (20 mg/kg q12h).

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: mucormycosis

clinical_record:
A 50-year-old Indian woman with diabetes and hypertension presented with right upper abdominal discomfort, loss of appetite, and low-grade fever. She denied jaundice.  
On examination, she had hepatomegaly and tenderness in the right hypochondrium.  
Laboratory studies showed normal liver-function tests. Serological tests for amoebiasis and hydatid disease were negative. A chest radiograph was normal.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an 11 × 7.5 × 11.2 cm predominantly anechoic, thick-walled lesion arising from the inferior surface of the liver, with low-level internal echoes and a homogeneous echogenic area in its superolateral portion. The gallbladder was not visualized separately; other abdominal viscera were normal.  
Aspiration of the lesion yielded turbid fluid, but the lesion persisted despite repeated aspirations and antibiotic therapy.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, lobulated cystic lesion with a solid component in its superior part, abutting the colon and duodenum. The lesion was interpreted as an infected non-parasitic cyst.

She initially sought evaluation for bloating but was advised to diet for presumed weight gain. She denied pain, vaginal bleeding, or systemic symptoms. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large, fluid-filled lesion measuring 19.3 × 6.2 × 21 cm, located in the pelvis and mid-abdomen, displacing the uterus and compressing the aorta and inferior vena cava. The lesion appeared unilocular with a 1.5 mm wall and no septations or solid components, and was suggestive of an ovarian origin.

A 55-year-old woman presented with generalized gum bleeding and halitosis. Her medical history was noncontributory, and she had undergone orthodontic treatment 18 years earlier. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Intraorally, there was generalized bleeding on probing and clinical attachment loss; radiographs showed generalized alveolar bone loss consistent with stage II, grade II periodontitis. Periapical radiographs of the maxillary central incisors revealed cervical areas of rarefaction. On endodontic evaluation, both central incisors were normal in color, responded normally to cold testing, and were asymptomatic to percussion and palpation. A 5 mm probing depth was recorded on the palatal aspects of both teeth. Two additional periapical radiographs with mesial and distal angulation showed that the lesion’s projection remained in the same position relative to the canal and that the canal outline was undisturbed. Cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated radiolucent resorptive lesions cervically on the palatal aspects of teeth #11 and #21, originating from the external palatal surface and perforating into the pulp space. The diagnosis for both central incisors was asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis with normal apical tissues and external cervical resorption.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a honeycomb-like tumor with solid components. PET–CT showed FDG uptake in the solid components of the cyst. From these imaging findings, the preoperative diagnosis of mucinous cystadenocarcinoma or sarcoma of the liver was made.
